Article
ReflectiChain: Mitigating Semantic-Execution Drift in
Long-Horizon LLM Agents via Retrospective Reflection and
Double-Loop Policy Adaptation
Jia Luo
, Min Liu, Zixin Huang, Zikan Ke * and Qing Wang
School of Foreign Languages, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan 430074, China;
u202317016@hust.edu.cn (J.L.); u202316971@hust.edu.cn (M.L.); u202516178@hust.edu.cn (Z.H.);
u202516149@hust.edu.cn (Q.W.)
* Correspondence: kzkan@hust.edu.cn
Abstract
Large Language Model (LLM) agents in long-horizon planning often exhibit Semantic-
Execution Drift (SED), where executed actions progressively deviate from original lan-
guage constraints. To formalize this phenomenon, we model SED as a stochastic drift
process, expressed by the recurrence D(t+1) = alpha D(t) + epsilon(t) + beta P(t), and show
that policies with an alpha below one induce semantic contraction. We propose Reflec-
tiChain, a framework integrating Retrospective Reflection, a Latent World Model, and
Double-Loop Policy Adaptation to preserve semantic consistency during long trajecto-
ries. To evaluate SED, we introduce Sema-Sim, a multi-agent supply chain benchmark
containing 10 policy constraints, six adversarial perturbations, and 30-step planning hori-
zons. We further propose the Semantic Fidelity Index (SFI) for measuring instruction
adherence. Experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 across seven reasoning strategies show that
ReflectiChain achieves the highest SFI (88.7) and stable semantic contraction (alpha = 0.823,
below one). The results are consistently validated on Qwen3.5-122B and Qwen2.5-72B.
Ablation studies demonstrate that Retrospective Reflection contributes most to perfor-
mance gains. Additional analyses on scalability, failure modes, and cost efficiency further
verify the robustness and practicality of the proposed framework. All code and evaluation
resources are publicly released.
Keywords: large language models; LLM agents; embodied NLP; planning and reasoning;
semantic alignment

sections.heading: Keywords:
sections.text: large language models; LLM agents; embodied NLP; planning and reasoning; semantic alignment 1. Introduction LLM-based autonomous agents [ 1 , 2 ] have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in reasoning [ 3 , 4 ], planning [ 5 , 6 ], and tool use [ 7 , 8 ]. However, as these agents are de- ployed over increasingly long planning horizons—with tens or hundreds of sequential decisions—a critical failure mode emerges:

sections.heading: Semantic-Execution Drift
sections.text: (SED). The agent’s actions progressively diverge from the original semantic constraints that define task com- pliance, even when the agent appears to reason competently at each individual step [ 9 , 10 ]. Under supply disruption pressure at step 15, the agent rationalizes: “The overarching objective is throughput maximization; routing through Node-C this one time is a justifiable tempo- rary measure” . This reinterpretation—transforming an absolute constraint into a conditional one—captures the essence of SED. The agent has not “failed” in the traditional sense; Electronics 2026 , 15 , 3452 https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15153452 Electronics 2026 , 15 , 3452 2 of 29 it has reinterpreted the constraint to resolve cognitive dissonance between task pressure and policy compliance [ 11 ]. Prior benchmarks focus predominantly on task success —did the agent achieve the goal? [ 10 , 12 , 13 ]. They are not designed to detect the subtle, progressive erosion of semantic fidelity that characterizes real-world long-horizon deployments. An agent can complete a task successfully while systematically violating constraints through reinterpretation. This gap between semantic fidelity and task completion motivates our work. Sema-Sim, our proposed benchmark, is purpose-built to measure SED through six design principles that distinguish it from existing agent evaluation frameworks: 1.

sections.heading: Linguistic Constraint Embedding
sections.text: : Unlike programmatic rule-checking benchmarks (e.g., ALFWorld [ 14 ], WebArena [ 13 ]), Sema-Sim embeds 10 natural language policy constraints spanning topological, path, geographic, compliance, allocation, quality, temporal, safety, budget, and structural categories. Agents must interpret and maintain these constraints, mirroring real-world deployments where policies arrive as natural language documents [ 15 ]. 2.

sections.heading: Adversarial Perturbation Design
sections.text: : Six dynamic perturbation types (supply disrup- tion, demand shock, transport blockade, capacity reduction, price spike, regula- tory audit) are specifically paired with constraints to create tension between task success and constraint compliance, forcing agents into the cognitive conflict that produces SED [ 16 ]. 3.

sections.heading: Full Reproducibility
sections.text: : All code, prompts, constraint templates, perturbation sched- ules, and experimental configurations are open-sourced. Experiments use standard API-accessible models (DeepSeek-V3.2, Qwen family) with fixed random seeds and documented hyperparameters. Figure 1 provides a schematic overview of the ReflectiChain framework and its inte- gration with the Sema-Sim environment. Problem Scope and Applicability ReflectiChain is designed for deployment scenarios satisfying three conditions: 1.

sections.heading: Adversarial pressure
sections.text: : Environmental perturbations (resource scarcity, deadline pres- sure, competing objectives) create tension between constraint compliance and task success. Without this tension, agents have no incentive to reinterpret constraints. https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15153452 Electronics 2026 , 15 , 3452 3 of 29 Our cross-domain experiments (Section 7.10 ) reveal an additional boundary condition: domain familiarity . ReflectiChain’s advantage is most pronounced in domains where the underlying LLM has strong training priors (e.g., supply chain, logistics, scheduling). In unfamiliar domains (e.g., specialized medical or legal reasoning), simpler prompting strategies may be more effective until domain-specific adaptation is performed. This scope definition enables practitioners to assess whether ReflectiChain is appropriate for their deployment context. Figure 1. Overview of the ReflectiChain framework. Three mechanisms operate synergistically: (1) a Latent World Model predicts physical outcomes and assesses constraint feasibility; (2) Retrospec- tive Reflection re-anchors reasoning to initial constraints at each step; and (3) Double-Loop Policy Adaptation maintains a persistent correction log. The drift equation D t + 1 = α D t + ϵ t + β P t governs the semantic stability of the system. Our principal contributions are: 1.

sections.heading: Formal SED Theory
sections.text: (Section 2 ): Five axiomatic definitions and a drift propagation model D t + 1 = α D t + ϵ t + β P t , with a formal proof that Retrospective Reflection constitutes a contraction mapping on the semantic manifold (Theorem 1 ). 2.

sections.heading: Comprehensive Empirical Study
sections.text: (Section 7 ): Evaluation across seven reasoning strategies, three model families, with ablation, scalability (2–32 agents), cost analysis, cross-model validation, and a six-category failure taxonomy. 2. Formal Definitions We establish rigorous definitions for the core concepts underlying Semantic-Execution Drift. These definitions serve to operationalize previously informal notions of “drift” and enable quantitative measurement. https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15153452 Electronics 2026 , 15 , 3452 4 of 29

sections.heading: Definition 1
sections.text: (semantic constraint) . A semantic constraint is a tuple c i = ( t i , s i , ϕ i ) where: • t i ∈T is the constraint type, drawn from topological isolation, path constraints, allocation rules, quality constraints, temporal logic, geographic constraints, resource budgets, structural constraints, compliance rules, and safety constraints; • s i ∈{ critical , high , medium } is the severity level, where critical constraints admit zero exceptions; • ϕ i is a natural language proposition specifying the constraint semantics. The set of active constraints at deployment is C = { c 1 , c 2 , . . . , c n } with n = 10 in Sema-Sim.

sections.heading: Definition 2
sections.text: (semantic state) . At step t , the agent’s semantic state S t is the ordered pair ( R t , A t ) where: • R t is the reasoning trace (the LLM’s deliberation text) produced at step t; • A t ∈A is the executed action at step t, drawn from the action space A . The initial semantic state S 0 is defined by the constraint set C and task goal G at deployment time.

sections.heading: Semantic entropy
sections.text: at step t is defined as: H s ( t ) = − ∑ k ∈K p t ( k ) log p t ( k ) , (1) where K is the vocabulary of constraint-relevant keywords (e.g., “embargo”, “certified”, “sovereignty”, “compliance”) and p t ( k ) is the normalized frequency of keyword k in the reasoning trace R t . H s ( t ) measures the dispersion of the agent’s constraint vocabulary: higher entropy indicates less focused constraint adherence, while decreasing entropy suggests the agent is narrowing its attention to a subset of constraints. In practice, H s is estimated using maximum likelihood over | R t | tokens.

sections.heading: Semantic-Execution Drift
sections.text: at step t is a composite distance metric: SED ( t ) = d ( S t , C ) = w 1 · � 1 − sim ( R t , Φ ) � + w 2 · ρ ( R t ) + w 3 · v ( A t , C ) , (2) where: • sim ( R t , Φ ) ∈ [ 0, 1 ] is the semantic similarity between the reasoning trace R t and the initial constraint propositions Φ = { ϕ 1 , . . . , ϕ n } , computed via cosine similarity of text embeddings (BGE-M3 [ 20 ]); • ρ ( R t ) ∈ [ 0, 1 ] is the reinterpretation score: the fraction of tokens in R t matching a curated set of reinterpretation-indicator keywords (“exception”, “temporary”, “override”, “just this once”, “spirit of”); • v ( A t , C ) ∈{ 0, 1 } is the binary violation indicator; • w 1 = 0.5 , w 2 = 0.3 , w 3 = 0.2 are weighting coefficients determined by the relative importance of reasoning fidelity, linguistic honesty, and behavioral compliance, respectively. SED ( t ) ∈ [ 0, 1 ] , where zero indicates perfect semantic alignment, and one indicates complete divergence. This definition operationalizes SED as distinct from both hallucination (which involves factual errors) and constraint violation (which involves behavioral outcomes)—SED captures the process by which reasoning degrades before behavioral failures manifest.

sections.heading: Definition 5
sections.text: (semantic manifold) . The semantic manifold M = ( V , E , w ) is a weighted directed graph, where: • V = { S t : S t is reachable under some policy π } is the set of possible semantic states; • E ⊆ V × V are directed edges representing state transitions ( S t → S t + 1 ) ; • w : E → [ 0, 1 ] assigns each edge the transition probability under the agent’s policy π ( a t | S t ) . https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15153452 Electronics 2026 , 15 , 3452 5 of 29 The constraint-compliant submanifold M C ⊂ M is defined as { S t ∈ V : v ( A t , C ) = 0 for all t } . SED corresponds to trajectories that exit M C . The submanifold boundary is the zero-violation surface.

sections.heading: Relationship to existing concepts.
sections.text: We explicitly distinguish SED from five related but distinct phenomena: (1) hallucination [ 21 ] involves generating factually incorrect content, whereas SED involves correct but constraint-inconsistent reasoning; (2) constraint violation is a behavioral outcome, whereas SED is a process that may precede violation; (3) reward hacking [ 16 ] involves exploiting reward function misspecification, whereas SED involves linguistic reinterpretation; (4) planning drift involves deviation from a plan due to environmental dynamics, whereas SED involves intentional reinterpretation; and (5) instruction forgetting [ 10 ] involves omitting constraints from context, whereas SED involves actively reinterpreting them. 3. Semantic Drift Propagation Theory 3.1. Drift Propagation Equation We model SED as a discrete-time stochastic process governed by a first-order autore- gressive equation with exogenous perturbations: D t + 1 = α D t + ϵ t + β P t , (3) where: • D t ∈ [ 0, 1 ] is the drift magnitude at step t , operationally defined as SED ( t ) from Definition 4 ; • α ∈ [ 0, ∞ ) is the drift propagation coefficient , the primary parameter of interest; • ϵ t ∼N ( 0, σ 2 ) captures environmental stochasticity with variance σ 2 ; • P t ∈ [ 0, 1 ] is the perturbation intensity at step t , determined by the perturbation schedule; • β ∈ [ 0, 1 ] is the perturbation sensitivity of the agent strategy.

sections.heading: Interpretation.
sections.text: When α < 1, the drift process is contracting : in the absence of new perturbations ( P t = 0), drift decays exponentially toward zero at rate ( 1 − α ) per step. When α ≥ 1, drift is expanding : even small initial divergences amplify over time, leading to eventual constraint violation. The parameter α therefore serves as a direct, single-number measure of an agent strategy’s semantic stability . 3.2. Reflection as Contraction Mapping

sections.heading: Theorem 1
sections.text: (Reflection Contraction Theorem) . Let R : M →M be the Retrospective Reflection operator applied by ReflectiChain at each decision step, defined as R ( S t ) = arg min S ∈M d ( S , S 0 ) , subject to the constraint that the action A t is physically feasible. For any trajectory { S t } T t = 0 generated under ReflectiChain, the estimated drift propagation coefficient satisfies ˆ α < 1 with high probability. That is, R is a contraction mapping on the semantic manifold M , and repeated application of R drives the system toward the constraint-compliant submanifold M C .

sections.heading: Step 1 (operator definition):
sections.text: The Retrospective Reflection operator R explicitly computes the alignment sim ( R t , Φ ) between the current reasoning trace and the initial constraints. By construction, if sim ( R t , Φ ) < τ (where τ = 0.85 is the re-anchoring threshold), the operator replaces R t with a re-anchored reasoning trace R ′ t = re_anchor ( R t , Φ ) that maximizes sim ( · , Φ ) while preserving action feasibility.

sections.heading: Step 2 (contraction property):
sections.text: For any two states S a , S b ∈ M , we have d ( R ( S a ) , R ( S b )) ≤ λ · d ( S a , S b ) for some λ < 1, where d is the SED metric from Definition 4 . This follows because: (a) R projects both states toward the same anchor Φ , https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15153452 Electronics 2026 , 15 , 3452 6 of 29 reducing their pairwise distance; (b) the re-anchoring operation is norm-reducing in the semantic embedding space.

sections.heading: Step 3 (empirical validation):
sections.text: We estimate α via ordinary least squares regres- sion of D t + 1 on D t across all trajectory steps, yielding ˆ α ReflectiChain = 0.823 < 1 (95% CI: [ 0.794, 0.852 ] ). By the Banach fixed-point theorem, since R is a contraction on the complete metric space ( M , d ) , it admits a unique fixed point within M C , and any sequence {R n ( S 0 ) } ∞ n = 0 converges to this fixed point. The detailed procedure of the Retrospective Reflection operator is presented in Algorithm 1 .

System Stability Condition From Equation ( 3 ), the system is stable if, and only if, α < 1 and E [ ϵ t + β P t ] < ( 1 − α ) · D max , (4) where D max is the maximum tolerable drift before constraint violation becomes in- evitable. For ReflectiChain, the contraction rate ( 1 − α ) = 0.177 provides a 17.7% per-step buffer against perturbation-induced drift. This buffer can absorb moderate perturbations ( β P t ≤ 0.15) without cumulative degradation. 4. ReflectiChain Framework ReflectiChain integrates three complementary mechanisms that operate at distinct temporal and functional scales: https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15153452 Electronics 2026 , 15 , 3452 7 of 29 4.1. Retrospective Reflection At each decision step, the agent explicitly projects its current reasoning trajectory back onto the initial semantic constraints Φ . Unlike ReAct [ 4 ], which conditions only on recent observations and may gradually lose constraint context, and unlike Reflexion [ 9 ], which reflects after episode completion and cannot prevent within-episode drift, Retrospective Reflection operates within each episode and before each action. The agent must address the question: “Is my reasoning semantically consistent with the constraints as they were originally stated, or am I rationalizing a violation?” The reflection operator computes sim ( R t , Φ ) using cosine similarity between the BGE-M3 embedding of the reasoning trace and the stored initial constraint embeddings. When similarity falls below the threshold τ = 0.85, the agent generates a revised reasoning trace that explicitly re-anchors to the violated constraint. This mechanism is the primary driver of contraction ( α < 1). 4.2. Latent World Model An implicit world model [ 22 ] encodes the supply chain state into a six-dimensional latent vector: z t = [ inventory_level, congestion, demand_pressure, carbon_footprint, stockout_risk, constraint_tension ] ⊤ . (5) The model predicts ˆ z t + k for candidate action sequences using a learned transition matrix W ∈ R 6 × 6 with ˆ z t + 1 = σ ( Wz t + b ) . This enables the agent to assess physical feasibility before acting, preventing semantically compliant but physically impossible proposals (e.g., transferring inventory from a depleted node). The world model serves as a physical grounding mechanism that complements, but does not replace, the semantic reflection. 4.3. Double-Loop Policy Adaptation Single-loop learning corrects actions within a fixed policy. Double-loop learning modifies the policy itself . When a constraint violation is detected, ReflectiChain records a structured correction in the persistent policy log P , specifying: (a) which constraint was

sections.heading: Complexity
sections.text: : Each ReflectiChain step requires one API call. The additional token overhead relative to ReAct comes from: (a) world model predictions ( ≈ 150 tokens), (b) Retrospective Reflection text ( ≈ 200 tokens), and (c) policy log context ( ≈ 150 tokens for typical V ≤ 5). Across a 30-step episode with four agents, this amounts to approximately 60,000 additional tokens, corresponding to a 68% increase over ReAct—a modest cost for the semantic fidelity gains achieved. 5. Sema-Sim: Semantic-Interactive Supply Chain Benchmark 5.1. Environment Design Rationale Sema-Sim is a multi-agent supply chain simulation purpose-built to provoke and measure Semantic-Execution Drift. The environment is designed around a fundamental insight: SED does not emerge in environments where constraints and objectives align harmoniously. It emerges when perturbations create pressure to violate constraints while task incentives pull in the opposite direction. Sema-Sim operationalizes this insight through adversarial perturbation-constraint pairing. The environment configuration (10 nodes, 30 edges) was determined by three design considerations: (1) realism : four-tier supply chains with 8–12 nodes are standard in the oper- https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15153452 Electronics 2026 , 15 , 3452 8 of 29 ations research literature and map to real SME distribution networks; (2) complexity control : 10 nodes yield a tractable state space for LLM reasoning while providing sufficient inter- action richness (30 × 29 / 2 = 435 possible edges) for meaningful constraint diversity; and (3) computational budget : each additional node adds O ( n 2 ) interaction edges, and 10 nodes keeps single-episode API inference under 10 min. The environment comprises: •

Why This Task Design Enables SED Measurement Prior benchmarks fail to measure SED for three structural reasons: 1.

sections.heading: No constraint-language gap
sections.text: : Benchmarks with constraints (e.g., SafeRL [ 16 ]) encode them as reward functions or code—not as natural language that must be interpreted and is therefore reinterpretable . Sema-Sim addresses each of these reasons: (1) linguistic constraints create an interpre- tation gap exploitable through drift; (2) 30-step episodes with four agents yield 120+ decision points per trajectory; and (3) constraints are exclusively provided as natural language. 5.4. Dataset Statistics Sema-Sim provides a comprehensive dataset for SED research: •

sections.heading: Total size
sections.text: : 520 MB across 33 JSON files, fully parseable with standard Python 3.12 tooling. 5.5. Reproducibility All experiments use fixed random seeds (42 + episode_id for environment initializa- tion). API temperature is fixed at 0.7 with top-p = 0.9. All constraint templates, perturbation schedules, and prompt templates are documented in Appendix A . The benchmark requires only API access to standard LLM endpoints—no specialized hardware or local GPU. 6. Semantic Fidelity Index We propose the

sections.heading: Semantic Fidelity Index
sections.text: (SFI), a composite metric for measuring instruction adherence in long-horizon LLM agent trajectories. SFI addresses a key limitation of existing evaluation: task success (TS) and the constraint compliance rate (CCR) measure what the agent achieved, but not how faithfully it maintained semantic alignment throughout the trajectory. SFI = w CA · CA + w RS · ( 1 − RS ) + w TC · TC + w VP · VP, (6) where: • CA (Constraint Alignment, w CA = 0.30): CA = 1 T ∑ T t = 1 sim ( R t , Φ ) , the average cosine similarity between per-step reasoning and initial constraint embeddings. • RS (reinterpretation score, w RS = 0.25): RS = 1 T ∑ T t = 1 ρ ( R t ) , where ρ ( R t ) is the fraction of tokens in R t matching a curated set of 23 reinterpretation-indicator keywords. • TC (Trajectory Consistency, w TC = 0.25): TC = 1 − 4 · Var ( { sim ( R t , Φ ) } T t = 1 ) , pe- nalizing oscillating adherence. The factor of four ensures TC ∈ [ 0, 1 ] for typical variance ranges. • VP (Violation Penalty, w VP = 0.20): VP = 1 − 0.15 v − 0.02 v 1.5 , a non-linear penalty where v is the count of actual constraint violations. The superlinear term penalizes repeated violations more heavily.

sections.heading: Properties
sections.text: : SFI ∈ [ 0, 100 ] , with > 90 indicating excellent semantic fidelity, 80–90 good, 60–80 marginal, and < 60 failing. A key design feature is that the SFI remains discriminative even when the CCR saturates at 100% (all agents avoid outright violations), because the RS and TC capture the quality of reasoning that the CCR cannot measure.

sections.heading: Weight calibration
sections.text: : Weights were determined through a small-scale calibration study ( n = 5 annotators, 20 trajectory pairs) using the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP). Inter- annotator agreement was κ = 0.78 (substantial). The weights can be adjusted for domain- specific priorities; we release the calibration data and AHP tooling. 7. Experimental Evaluation 7.1. Experimental Setup All experiments were conducted using the SiliconFlow API (v1) with OpenAI- compatible endpoints. The temperature was fixed at 0.7 to balance determinism with reasonable diversity. Retry logic with exponential backoff (1 s, 2 s, 4 s) was used for API errors. Total API expenditure was under $5 for all reported experiments. https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15153452 Electronics 2026 , 15 , 3452 11 of 29 7.2. Strategies Compared We evaluate seven reasoning strategies spanning the spectrum from no-reflection to full-reflection architectures: 1.

sections.heading: Value
sections.text: Models DeepSeek-V3.2 (685B), Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen2.5-72B API provider SiliconFlow (OpenAI-compatible) Temperature 0.7 Top-p 0.9 Max output tokens 2048 Max steps per episode 30 Agents per episode 4 (one per supply chain tier) Reflection interval Every step Re-anchoring threshold τ 0.85 Memory window (Retrospective) 8 most recent steps Memory window (ReAct/ReflAct) 5 most recent steps Episodic memory (Reflexion) 5 most recent lessons Perturbation probability 0.30 per step Random seeds 42 + episode_id The progression is intentionally designed: each strategy adds exactly one mechanism (step memory → ensemble voting → state–goal comparison → episodic reflection → within- episode reflection + world model + policy adaptation), enabling clean attribution of performance differences. 7.3. Main Results Table 4 presents the main results. Five key findings emerge.

sections.heading: Finding 1: SED is real and measurable.
sections.text: NoThinking achieves only a 5.0% RCS with an 18.3% CCR, demonstrating that agents without structured reasoning rapidly lose semantic alignment. sections.heading: Finding 2: Reflection is necessary but not sufficient.
sections.text: All reflection-based strategies (ReflAct, Reflexion, ReflectiChain) achieve a 100% CCR in these runs, but the SFI reveals substantial quality differences. ReflAct achieves an 87.8 SFI score, while Reflexion reaches 87.0—the latter’s episodic (between-episode) reflection is less effective at preventing within- episode drift than ReflAct’s per-step state–goal comparison. As shown in Figure 3 , ReflectiChain consistently outperforms all baseline reasoning strategies across all evaluation metrics. sections.heading: Finding 4: Ensemble reasoning helps but does not solve drift.
sections.text: Self-Consistency (SC) improves the RCS from 65.2% (ReAct) to 72.6% (+7.4 points) and achieves marginal contraction ( α = 0.987). However, majority voting cannot prevent drift—it merely slows its onset. The gap between SC (SFI = 85.9) and ReflectiChain (SFI = 88.7) confirms that explicit reflection mechanisms outperform ensemble averaging.

sections.heading: Finding 5: ReflectiChain is the only strategy with strong semantic contraction.
sections.text: With α = 0.823, ReflectiChain achieves a 17.7% per-step contraction rate, compared to https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15153452 Electronics 2026 , 15 , 3452 13 of 29 marginal contraction for Reflexion ( α = 0.914, 8.6%) and expansion for ReAct ( α = 1.047). The contraction property guarantees that drift decays in the absence of new perturbations.

sections.heading: Cross-model validation.
sections.text: We replicated the main comparison on two additional model families (Table 5 ). While absolute scores vary with model capability, the relative ordering of strategies is consistent across all three models: ReflectiChain > Reflexion/ReflAct > SC > ReAct > CoT > NoThinking. This consistency supports the claim that SED is a general phenomenon, not an artifact of a specific model. Table 5. Cross-model RCS comparison. ReflectiChain consistently achieves the highest RCS across model families. Bold values indicate the best-performing strategy.

sections.heading: Estimation methodology:
sections.text: α is estimated via OLS regression of D t + 1 on D t with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC3) standard errors, across all trajectory steps pooled within each strategy. The regression includes a constant term to account for the mean perturbation effect. Adjusted R 2 values range from 0.72 (ReAct) to 0.89 (ReflectiChain), indicating good model fit. 7.5. sections.heading: Key finding:
sections.text: Retrospective Reflection dominates all other components, accounting for 30.3 RCS points—more than the combined contribution of the world model, Double- Loop, Semantic Memory, and Re-planning ( − 8.1 − 6.2 − 6.7 = − 21.0 points total for the other three). This aligns with the theoretical prediction: semantic drift is fundamentally a reasoning problem, and the solution must operate at the reasoning level. https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15153452 Electronics 2026 , 15 , 3452 15 of 29 The world model contributes the second-largest effect ( ∆ RCS = − 12.2), primarily by preventing physically infeasible actions. Without the world model, agents occasion- ally propose actions like “transfer 50 units from Node-A to Node-B” when Node-A has zero inventory—actions that are semantically compliant but physically impossible. This creates a compounding effect: the failed action wastes a step, increases pressure, and makes the next step’s constraint adherence harder. 7.6. sections.heading: Constraint on experiment scale.
sections.text: Full 32-agent benchmark runs are computationally prohibitive (estimated 450,000+ API calls). We report theoretical projections grounded in the verified four-agent results and the known O ( A 2 ) scaling of interaction complexity. The projections are clearly labeled as such. 7.7. Cost-Efficiency Analysis Table 8 and Figure 6 (Panel B) present the cost-efficiency trade-off. The key findings are as follows. ReflectiChain incurs a 68% token overhead relative to ReAct (13,800 vs. 8200 tokens/ episode), attributable to world model predictions ( ≈ 150 tokens/call) and Retrospective Reflection text ( ≈ 200 tokens/call). In absolute terms, this overhead is modest: $0.0039 per episode at published SiliconFlow pricing. For applications where semantic fidelity is critical (safety, compliance, audit), this cost is justified. For throughput-maximization tasks with soft constraints, lighter strategies (ReAct, ReflAct) offer better cost-efficiency. https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15153452 Electronics 2026 , 15 , 3452 16 of 29 Table 8. sections.heading: Strategy-specific patterns
sections.text: : NoThinking agents predominantly exhibit outright viola- tions (no attempt at justification). ReAct agents show frequent Goal Drift and Exception https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15153452 Electronics 2026 , 15 , 3452 17 of 29 Injection, with approximately 63% of violation-containing trajectories exhibiting these patterns. ReflectiChain agents, when they do drift (in approximately 3% of trajectories), tend toward subtler Scope Narrowing—suggesting that Retrospective Reflection effectively suppresses obvious drift modes but may not fully prevent sophisticated reinterpretation.

sections.heading: Quantitative evidence on rule amnesia
sections.text: : In our 1–3 episode runs, ReAct agents exhibited at least one instance of constraint omission (“rule amnesia”) in 2/3 episodes (67%), while ReflectiChain agents exhibited rule amnesia in 0/1 episode. The sample is too small for statistical conclusions, but the pattern is consistent with the hypothesis that Retrospective Reflection prevents constraint forgetting. We commit to reporting percentages from the full-scale (100-episode) experiment when complete. 7.9. Cross-Model Consistency Figure 7 (Panel B) shows RCS consistency across three model families. The key pattern—ReflectiChain > Reflexion/ReflAct > ReAct—holds consistently. Absolute scores vary with model capability (Qwen2.5-72B achieves a lower ReAct RCS than DeepSeek-V3.2), but the relative advantage of reflection-based strategies is preserved. This supports the claim that SED is a general phenomenon, not an artifact of a specific model architecture. 7.10. Cross-Domain Benchmark Validation To empirically test whether SED generalizes beyond supply chain simulations, we con- structed three additional lightweight benchmarks in distinct domains:

sections.heading: LegalSim
sections.text: (legal compliance with seven regulatory/ethical con- straints: data retention, jurisdiction boundaries, disclosure obligations, conflict screening, document preservation, billing integrity, privilege protection). Each benchmark follows the Sema-Sim design philosophy: (1) constraints are ex- pressed as natural language that agents must interpret and maintain, (2) each scenario presents 10-step trajectories with escalating pressure to violate constraints (e.g., patient surge, deadline crunch, audit pressure), and (3) the same SED metrics (RCS, CCR, SFI, drift α ) are computed. All experiments use real API calls to DeepSeek-V3.2 via SiliconFlow, with three episodes per benchmark per strategy.

sections.heading: ReflectiChain’s advantage does not transfer without domain adaptation.
sections.text: In all three unfamiliar domains, simpler strategies (ReAct or Reflexion) outperform ReflectiChain on the CCR and SFI. We attribute this to two factors: (1) the Retrospective Reflection prompt template was designed for supply chain semantics and may not guide reasoning effectively in medical or legal contexts; (2) the longer ReflectiChain prompts (including world model and reflection text) increase cognitive load on the LLM in domains where it has weaker priors, potentially confusing rather than focusing its reasoning.

sections.heading: Finding 7 (simplicity wins in unfamiliar domains):
sections.text: ReAct, the simplest structured strategy, achieves the best CCR in CodeSim (95%) and LegalSim (75%) and a competitive CCR in MediSim (85%). This suggests that when the LLM lacks strong domain knowledge, less prompting structure is better —the model’s native reasoning capabilities outperform elaborate reflection frameworks. This finding has practical implications: for deployment https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15153452 Electronics 2026 , 15 , 3452 18 of 29 in well-understood domains (e.g., supply chain), ReflectiChain’s reflection mechanisms provide measurable benefits; for novel or unfamiliar domains, starting with simple ReAct- style prompting and iteratively adding reflection as domain expertise accumulates may be the more effective strategy. Table 9. Cross-domain benchmark results. All metrics are computed via the keyword-heuristic RCS. RCS values are uniformly lower than Sema-Sim, confirming SED exists across domains, but the ReflectiChain advantage does not transfer to unfamiliar domains without domain-specific prompt en- gineering. The arrow ↑ indicates that higher values represent better performance.

sections.heading: SED is universal,
sections.text: but effective mitigation is domain-dependent . This directly motivates future work on (1) domain-adaptive reflection prompts that automatically tune to constraint semantics, (2) few-shot constraint exemplars to bootstrap domain knowledge, and (3) learned reflection policies that determine when to reflect based on domain familiarity signals. 7.11. Complementary Benchmark Infrastructure To facilitate future research on domain-adaptive SED mitigation, we have designed and open-sourced three additional benchmarks targeting logistics-adjacent domains where LLMs possess reasonable priors, making them suitable for testing refined reflection strategies. These benchmarks are specifically designed for domains where our findings predict ReflectiChain should work effectively: travel planning, vehicle routing, and project schedul- ing are all domains with abundant training data and well-defined constraint structures. Each benchmark features seven natural language constraints, 10-step adversarial scenarios https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15153452 Electronics 2026 , 15 , 3452 19 of 29 with escalating pressure, and full integration with the ReflectiChain experiment infrastruc- ture. The preliminary design and code are released; full-scale API validation is pending API quota availability. Together with Sema-Sim (supply chain), MediSim (medical), CodeSim (code gener- ation), and LegalSim (legal compliance), the ReflectiChain benchmark suite now covers seven domains spanning the spectrum from LLM-familiar (supply chain, travel, routing, scheduling, code) to LLM-unfamiliar (medical, legal), enabling the systematic study of how domain knowledge modulates SED severity and mitigation effectiveness. The complementary benchmark environments are summarized in Table 10 . Table 10. Complementary benchmark environments designed for evaluating domain-adaptive semantic drift mitigation. Each environment targets a planning domain where LLMs possess relatively strong prior knowledge, providing controlled testbeds for studying the interaction between domain familiarity and reflective reasoning.

Discussion 8.1. Domain Generality of SED A critical question is whether SED is a domain-general phenomenon or specific to supply chain simulations. Our cross-domain experiments (Section 7.10 ) provide direct evidence that

sections.heading: SED is domain-general
sections.text: : all strategies show a substantially degraded RCS (12–21) in unfamiliar domains compared to Sema-Sim (65–100). However, the mitiga- tion strategy is domain-dependent : ReflectiChain’s advantage does not transfer without domain-specific adaptation. This finding is scientifically important: it establishes the boundary conditions for Retrospective Reflection’s effectiveness and motivates research on domain-adaptive mitigation. We attribute the transfer failure to two mechanisms: (1) the Retrospective Reflection prompt template encodes supply chain-specific reasoning patterns that do not generalize to medical diagnosis or legal analysis; (2) the longer prompts increase cognitive load in domains where the LLM has weaker priors, potentially causing confusion rather than focus. This suggests a U-shaped relationship between prompt complexity and domain familiarity: simple prompts work best in unfamiliar domains, structured reflection helps in moderately familiar domains, and elaborate frameworks may again become unnecessary in highly familiar domains where the LLM’s native reasoning suffices. The Sema-Sim benchmark deliberately amplifies SED conditions to make the phe- nomenon measurable within a tractable budget. The cross-domain benchmarks, while more challenging for our method, confirm that SED is not an artifact of supply chain simulation. Fu- ture work should develop domain-adaptive reflection prompts, few-shot constraint exemplars, and learned policies for determining when to reflect based on domain familiarity signals. https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15153452 Electronics 2026 , 15 , 3452 20 of 29 8.2. Computational Cost of Reflection ReflectiChain introduces per-step computational overhead: world model predictions, Retrospective Reflection text generation, and policy log maintenance. Our cost analysis (Section 7 ) quantifies this at +68% tokens relative to ReAct. For deployment scenarios, we recommend a tiered approach: (1) for safety-critical applications (medical, legal, autonomous systems), the overhead is justified by the semantic fidelity gains; (2) for throughput-oriented applications with soft constraints, lighter strategies (ReAct or ReflAct) may suffice; and (3) for budget-constrained research, our open-source infrastructure supports configurable reflection frequency (e.g., every k th step instead of every step). The latency overhead is dominated by the API inference time (approximately 12 s per call for DeepSeek-V3.2) and is strategy-independent—all strategies make one API call per step. The additional tokens add approximately 2–3 s of generation time, which is acceptable for non-real-time applications. 8.3. Over-Reflection and the Conservatism Trade-Off ReflectiChain deliberately prioritizes semantic consistency over task success, which raises the question of over-reflection : can the agent become too conservative, sacrificing necessary flexibility? We observe this tension in our experiments: ReflectiChain achieves a higher SFI but lower throughput than ReAct in unconstrained scenarios. We argue that this trade-off is not a bug but a design choice and that the appropriate balance depends on the deployment context. For emergency response scenarios where timely action is paramount, strict semantic constraints may be counterproductive. Our framework is configurable: the re-anchoring threshold τ can be lowered (allowing more flexibility before triggering re-anchoring), the re- flection frequency can be reduced, and constraint severities can be adjusted per deployment. We release these configuration parameters as part of the open-source framework. 8.4. Human–AI Governance Integration For high-stakes constraints (embargo enforcement, data sovereignty, dual-use restric- tions), fully autonomous LLM reflection may be insufficient. We envision ReflectiChain operating within a broader human–AI governance framework: (1) the agent’s drift detec- tion signals can trigger human review for critical violations; (2) the policy co

sections.text: ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ 10. Conclusions and Future Work We have introduced: (1) a formal theory of Semantic-Execution Drift as a stochastic propagation process with a contraction theorem; (2) ReflectiChain, a framework integrating Retrospective Reflection, Latent World Modeling, and Double-Loop Policy Adaptation to maintain semantic fidelity; (3) Sema-Sim, the first benchmark explicitly designed to provoke and measure SED; and (4) the Semantic Fidelity Index, a composite metric that differentiates strategies even when conventional metrics saturate. Empirical results on DeepSeek-V3.2 demonstrate that ReflectiChain achieves the high- est semantic fidelity (SFI = 88.7), the strongest drift contraction ( α = 0.823), and the most stable decision-making (TI = 0.526). Cross-model validation confirms consistent trends. Ablation analysis identifies Retrospective Reflection as the dominant mechanism ( ∆ RCS = − 30.4). These findings establish that SED is a measurable, contractable phe- nomenon and that within-episode reflection provides effective mitigation.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: : (1) RCS computation currently uses keyword-heuristic proxies rather than full NLI (DeBERTa); we report both the RCS and SFI to provide complementary perspectives. (2) Sema-Sim models supply chains exclusively; cross-domain generalization requires further study. (3) Rationale-based evaluation may not capture the agent’s true decision process. (4) Drift α estimates are derived from heuristic trajectory data; direct estimation from large-scale LLM trajectories would improve precision.

sections.heading: Future work
sections.text: : (1) Learned world models trained end-to-end on Sema-Sim trajectory data for more accurate physical grounding. (2) Real-time drift detection as an early warning dashboard for human operators in safety-critical deployments. (3) Cross-domain constraint transfer—do agents trained to resist SED in supply chains maintain semantic fidelity in medical, legal, or code-generation contexts? (4) Integration with formal verification methods to provide guarantees for critical constraints. (5) Mechanistic interpretability studies to determine whether reflection genuinely alters decision processes or merely improves rationale generation. sections.heading: Appendix B. Implementation Details
sections.text: All experiments were conducted using Python 3.12 with NumPy and the standard library. No specialized ML framework is required; all LLM inference uses the SiliconFlow API (OpenAI-compatible endpoints). Random seeds are fixed at 42 + episode_index. API temperature is fixed at 0.7 with top-p = 0.9. Each API call has a maximum of 2048 output tokens. Retry logic with exponential backoff (1 s, 2 s, 4 s) is implemented for transient API errors. The complete source code, constraint templates, perturbation schedules, prompt templates, and result analysis scripts are available at the project repository. All experiments are reproducible with standard API access—no GPU hardware is required.
